synopsis.statement: swe-prep is a single-user interview-prep app that runs your code. Its product is a daily session in three tiers: a required ~4-minute warm-up of ~8 quick reps that alone completes the day, an optional ~30-minute main exercise, then uncapped continuation. Everything under it - the grader/runner seam, the spaced-repetition queue, the empirical complexity check, the readiness surface - exists to make that daily loop cheap enough to never skip and honest enough to believe.

evidence.note: the three-tier session decision

nodes.title: Where it runs, and what it is built with
nodes.question: Where does swe-prep run, and what is it built with?
nodes.decision: A local web app: Spring Boot on Java 21, Postgres, React + Vite, Monaco. Reached over a tailnet, autostarted as a systemd user unit. Not hosted.
nodes.why: Front-end practice is a named future domain, and grading it means rendering and asserting in a browser. A web app is the only shape that holds every named domain without a second platform later. The choice was made on domain coverage, not on friction - a TUI would genuinely have had the lowest friction for a heavy terminal user, and the friction cost was paid off separately with autostart.

rejected.why_it_lost: explicitly the lowest-friction option for a heavy terminal user, and still rejected because it can never grade front-end work.
would have to embed a browser to fake the same capability.
its only real advantage was needing no service, which is worth little against something already configured - and Postgres removes any migration if the app is ever hosted.

nodes.divergence: The decision names Spring Boot 3.4.3 with Spring Data JPA and Lombok. What shipped is spring-boot-starter-jdbc with JdbcClient, no Lombok, on Boot 3.4.7. The divergence is now acknowledged on the decision issue itself.
nodes.soundbite: I chose the shape by which domains it could still hold in a year, not by what was fastest to open today, and then paid off the friction cost separately with autostart.

nodes.title: The exercise and runner abstraction
nodes.question: What is the exercise/runner abstraction, so that every named domain fits without a redesign?
nodes.decision: Split Grader from Runner - a Grader decides pass or fail, a Runner only executes - and make test cases language-neutral JSON data with a per-language harness.
nodes.why: The obvious design makes Exercise mean "thing that runs code", after which concepts and warm-up reps become special cases bolted on the side. Separating what the user produces from how it is judged is what stops "exercise" from secretly meaning "code": a concept question has a Grader and no Runner at all. Writing test cases as JUnit would mean every new language re-authors the entire problem set - that is the difference between pluggable languages being real and being aspirational.

rejected.alternative: Exercise as a code-execution type, with concepts as special cases
rejected.why_it_lost: makes every non-code domain a bolt-on and forecloses SQL, concepts and front end in one move.

rejected.alternative: Test cases authored as JUnit tests
rejected.why_it_lost: every new language would require re-authoring the entire problem set.
LeetCode's existing convention ([1,2,3,null,4]) is adopted instead, since the captain reads their statements anyway.

nodes.divergence: The decision names five Response kinds - Choice, ShortAnswer, Program, Query and "later, Component". The sealed interface at this SHA permits Code, Choice, FreeText and Query. Component is absent, which is the front-end domain being genuinely unbuilt rather than renamed.
nodes.soundbite: A Grader decides pass or fail; a Runner only executes. Once those are apart, a concept question is not a special case - it is just an exercise with no Runner.

nodes.title: How a submission is judged
nodes.question: How is a submission judged, and what does the app tell you when it fails?
nodes.decision: Correctness is pass/fail with no partial credit; on failure the app reports only how many tests failed; help (hints, the failing case) is always available, always recorded, never penalised; a complexity claim is stated before the target is revealed and then checked by measuring scaling empirically.
nodes.why: Re-reading your own code and reasoning about it without an oracle is the skill a real interview tests, and an app that always hands over the failing case trains the opposite reflex. Penalties on a self-imposed system only teach the user to game themselves. A self-report alone would congratulate an O(n^2) solution claiming to be O(n) - the single case most worth catching - so the claim is scored against measurement rather than an honour-system checkbox.

rejected.why_it_lost: would invent a number that means nothing and soften the only honest signal available.
trains the opposite of the interview skill - it is why people grind hundreds of problems and still freeze.
on a self-imposed system, penalties only teach the user to game themselves.
noise, and not what interviews reject people over.
would punish JVM warm-up and teach nothing; runtime is reported for interest only.

implemented_by.note: Verdict carries passed/total and nothing about a case

nodes.soundbite: The failure response is deliberately impoverished. Verdict carries passed and total - no input, no expected, no actual - unless you explicitly ask, and asking is recorded and never costs you anything.

"Can you really measure complexity by timing?"

nodes.question: Can Blind 75 problem statements ship in a public repository?
nodes.decision: Public engine, private content. No problem statement, test case, reference solution or generator lives in this repository; content is loaded at runtime from a gitignored local clone of a separate private repo.
nodes.why: The private-solutions decision had already collapsed this question: once solutions are private, the statements have to travel with them, and the engine is the part worth showing publicly anyway. Making it a repository boundary rather than a policy means the rule can be checked mechanically instead of remembered.

rejected.why_it_lost: the copyright position on redistributing problem statements is not one worth defending on a portfolio project.

nodes.soundbite: The boundary is not a policy, it is a repository split with a CI script that fails the build on three separate leak shapes - and that script has its own tests.

nodes.title: How the app chooses what you practise next
nodes.question: How does the app choose what you practise next?
nodes.decision: Two schedulers over one shared attempt record: a standard SM-2 due-date queue for reps, and a priority score - not a due date - for challenges, with a hard minimum-interval floor and a weekly cap on new introductions.
nodes.why: Spaced repetition assumes reviews are cheap. Twenty due Anki cards cost four minutes; twenty due 30-40 minute challenges is a fortnight of work, and a scheduler that generates impossible debt gets ignored within a week. The scarcity is structural too - roughly 90 challenge slots exist in three months against ~75 problems. Due dates ask what is owed; a priority score asks what is worth it, and only the second survives scarcity.

rejected.why_it_lost: SM-2's arithmetic breaks completely at 30-40 minutes per review; it would generate debt that cannot be paid.
better on paper, marginal at one user and ~400 reps; keep the algorithm swappable and do not agonise.

rejected.alternative: Feeding raw attempt fields into the algorithms
rejected.why_it_lost: collapsing to a 0-5 quality score keeps the scheduler from ossifying around today's exact recorded fields.

rejected.alternative: Including time taken as a signal
rejected.why_it_lost: interruptions, thinking before typing, and typing fast on a misunderstood problem all corrupt it - variance without information.
nothing is ever deleted; a problem passed cleanly three times earns an interval of months. That is retirement, not removal.

implemented_by.note: the two gates return OptionalDouble.empty(), not a low score

nodes.divergence: The decision's "interview soon" mode - a re-weighted scoring function for the final fortnight that drops the minimum-interval floor - is not built at this SHA. A case-insensitive search of backend/src and frontend/src for interview-soon / interviewSoon / InterviewMode returns nothing.
nodes.soundbite: Due dates ask what is owed; a priority score asks what is worth it. At 40 minutes a review, only the second one survives.

nodes.title: The language-neutral claim, now demonstrated rather than intended
nodes.what: A second language adapter (PythonLanguageAdapter + LocalPythonRunner) grades the literal same in-memory Exercise fixture that Java grades, with zero content changes. LanguageAdapterRegistry and RunnerRegistry route a plain language string to the one adapter and runner that target it; Java is always first and is the default when the language is null, blank or omitted.
nodes.why_interesting: This is the project's central design claim - a test case authored once runs in every language - moving from a design intention to a demonstrated property. The proof is deliberately not a Python-flavoured copy of the fixture: TestCaseGraderTest.aSecondLanguageSolvesTheExactSameStoredExerciseWithNoContentChange runs the same object through the Python path. What the ticket also surfaced is the honest part: adding the second language forced real changes to engine code the single-adapter version had left implicitly Java-only (submissionFileName(), languageId(), a submission.language column), and none to content.
gotchas: Map.copyOf does not preserve iteration order (explicitly unspecified for 2+ entries), which would silently undo the Java-first sort. The registry sorts into a LinkedHashMap and wraps it with Collections.unmodifiableMap instead.

Python's indentation is syntactically significant, so PythonLanguageAdapter does not reuse Java's text-block-with-.formatted() splicing style - every emitted line carries its own explicit absolute indentation.

LocalPythonRunner reports COMPILE_ERROR only for a genuine syntax error (python3 -m py_compile). A NameError at runtime surfaces as a per-case "threw" failure, which is an honest difference from Java's stricter compile step, not a gap to close.

interviewer_questions.question: "How would you add Python?"
interviewer_questions.answer: One LanguageAdapter and one Runner. Zero test cases are re-authored, because they are language-neutral JSON - and that is now demonstrated, not claimed: the same stored exercise is graded through Python in a test.

interviewer_questions.question: "How do you support more than one language?"
interviewer_questions.answer: Two registries route a language string to the one adapter and runner that target it, Java first and default. Adding the second language changed engine code and no content.

evidence.note: the same stored exercise, graded through Python

nodes.title: The Grader / Runner seam, and boundaries kept in the type system
nodes.what: GraderRegistry receives List<Grader> from Spring and routes each exercise by the grader's own supports(). TestCaseGrader takes an adapter registry and a runner registry; AnswerKeyGrader's constructor takes only an ObjectMapper and has no Runner field at all; SelfCheckGrader is a routed Grader bean whose grade() throws.
nodes.why_interesting: The abstraction decision said the split exists. The codebase then refuses to let a caller violate it. AnswerKeyGrader having no Runner field is the mechanically checkable existence proof that the split is real rather than naming, and SelfCheckGrader.grade() throwing makes "a self-rating never reaches the spaced-repetition quality score" an unrepresentable state instead of a comment and some discipline.
gotchas: The same boundary is defended a second time in SQL: a self-check does write a row, always as SubmissionOutcome.SELF_RATED, which is a superset of Verdict.Outcome and deliberately not a member of it. Every competence query filters on outcome = 'PASSED'.
Adding a grading kind is a new bean plus one more permitted record - there is nothing in the registry to change.

nodes.title: Public engine, private content - and the guard that keeps it true
nodes.what: scripts/check-no-content.sh runs first in CI and first in ./test.sh and fails the build on three independent leak shapes: anything tracked under content/; content/ not being gitignored at all (checked with git check-ignore against a probe path, so the rule cannot silently lapse); and any tracked *.json that looks like content - an exercise carrying both "statement" and "grading", or a lesson carrying "kind":"lesson" or both "statement" and "checks".
nodes.why_interesting: The licensing decision is only as good as its enforcement, and "remember not to commit content" is not enforcement. The second check is the interesting one: it does not check that content/ is absent, it checks that the ignore rule still exists, so the guard cannot be defeated by someone quietly editing .gitignore. The script has its own test file, so the guard is itself guarded.
gotchas: The leak-shape grep is why the content-authoring tool's ProblemSpec format is deliberately not shaped like a real exercise JSON: a problem-spec fixture can never carry both "statement" and "grading", so committing one as a test resource cannot trip the guard.

interviewer_questions.question: "Where is the content? This repo has no problems in it."
interviewer_questions.answer: Correct, by design and by CI. A guard script fails the build on three independent leak shapes, including one that checks the gitignore rule still exists - and the guard has its own tests.

nodes.title: Empirical complexity measurement, and refusing to overclaim
nodes.what: After a passing submission the solver states time and space complexity before the authored target is revealed, and the time claim is checked by timing the submission at growing input sizes and fitting a log-log regression. ComplexityBucket collapses the claim vocabulary to five buckets the measurement can actually discriminate - CONSTANT and LOGARITHMIC share SUBLINEAR, LINEAR and LINEARITHMIC share LINEAR.
nodes.why_interesting: The bucket collapse is the honesty constraint expressed as a type rather than as a caution in the docs: a linear claim can never be contradicted by a linearithmic measurement because they are the same bucket. MeasurementOutcome is sealed Skipped | Inconclusive | Conclusive, so "inconclusive" is a first-class result and not an else-branch, and even Conclusive is never worded "correct" by the caller - only "consistent with measurement".
gotchas: JIT dead-code elimination: a trivial loop's return value, if never consumed, can get the whole call eliminated by C2. The timing harness stashes every result into a static Object sink inside the timed window specifically to defeat this.

JIT/vectorisation warm-up: a cheap auto-vectorisable op can show its first few calls an order of magnitude slower than later ones. The harness makes untimed warm-up calls first, then takes the median (not min, not mean) across timed calls per size.
ScalingMeasurer is not a new Runner method - it is a different generated harness run through the same Runner.execute(), so it inherits the exact isolation and timeout every other execution gets.

interviewer_questions.question: "Can you really measure complexity by timing?"
interviewer_questions.answer: Only coarsely, and the code says so. Buckets collapse O(n) and O(n log n) into one class so a claim can never be contradicted on a distinction timing cannot make, and "inconclusive" is a first-class result.

interviewer_questions.question: "What is the hardest bug you hit?"
interviewer_questions.answer: The JIT eliminating the timed call as dead code, and vectorisation warm-up making the first calls an order of magnitude slower. Both only appeared in real execution; the fixes are a static sink inside the timed window and a median across timed calls after untimed warm-ups.

evidence.note: javadoc documents both JIT effects as found by real execution

nodes.title: Three derivations over one attempt record, deliberately not merged
nodes.what: LearnedCriterion ("has this been retrieved to criterion?"), RepDueService via Sm2Scheduler ("is this rep due today?") and ChallengePriority ("what is the best use of 40 minutes today?") all read the same attempt and submission history and never read each other. All three are recomputed on read; none is a stored row.
nodes.why_interesting: The non-relationships matter as much as the relationships. Merging them looks like deduplication and is actually a category error - they answer three different questions and are tuned independently on purpose. Because everything is derived on read there is no second source of truth to drift, which is the whole answer to "how do you keep spaced-repetition state consistent?".
gotchas: The objective competence signal is the SQL predicate outcome = 'PASSED', repeated across SubmissionRepository's queries. A self-check writes SELF_RATED and a lesson read writes no submission at all, so neither can ever satisfy that filter - the boundary is in the query, not in a caller's discipline.

challengeReviews' filter is one outcome wider than repReviews' (it includes EXPLAINED) because a self-check challenge never ends SOLVED or ABANDONED; omitting it would leave such a challenge permanently invisible to the scorer.
interviewer_questions: "How do you keep the spaced-repetition state consistent?"

evidence.note: the outcome = 'PASSED' boundary, in two queries

nodes.title: The suite is red at this commit, and the cause is a real bug
nodes.statement: ./test.sh fails at this SHA. ReadinessServiceTest.staleTopicsFlagsATopicNotTouchedRecentlyAndSkipsAnUntouchedOne expected 30 days and got 31. The cause is that ReadinessService takes an injected Clock but then calls LocalDate.now(zone) - the wall clock - for "today", instead of LocalDate.now(clock). Every other site in the codebase (SessionService, ChallengeService, RepDueService, DeterministicOptionShuffler) uses LocalDate.now(clock); readiness is the lone outlier, so the stale-topic day count is wall-clock dependent and the test only passes when run early enough in the day.
nodes.why_it_matters: It is a one-line fix, and it is worth going first on because the whole point of the injected Clock bean is that day boundaries are testable. A reviewer who greps for LocalDate.now( finds it in about ten seconds.
nodes.how_to_say_it: The suite is red at the commit I am showing you, and I know exactly why: readiness reads the wall clock where every other date-sensitive service reads the injected one. It is a one-line fix and I verified it - I would rather show you the commit with the bug in it and the diagnosis than a cherry-picked green one.

interviewer_questions.question: "Does it build?"
interviewer_questions.answer: Not at this commit, and I know why: readiness reads the wall clock where every other date-sensitive service reads the injected one. 466 tests, 1 failure, 5 skipped. It is a one-line fix.

nodes.title: The front-end domain is decided and specified, and nothing is built
nodes.statement: The abstraction decision names a Component response graded by a headless-browser runner with DOM assertions, and states plainly that the JSON-test-case model does not extend to it. nodes.title: The build diverges from the written stack decision, and the record now says so
nodes.statement: Decision #2 names Spring Boot 3.4.3 with Spring Data JPA and Lombok. The build is Boot 3.4.7 with spring-boot-starter-jdbc, JdbcClient and no Lombok. A follow-up comment on issue #2 records the divergence on the decision itself.
nodes.why_it_matters: The queries here are read-shaped derivations over two tables, not object graphs, and records already gave the mapping - so the divergence is defensible. It is also a divergence from a written decision, and Spring Data JPA is what entry-level Java postings screen for, so both halves of the answer need to be ready.
nodes.how_to_say_it: I decided JPA and shipped JdbcClient, and I wrote that down on the decision rather than quietly leaving the record wrong. Every query in this codebase is a read-shaped derivation, not an object graph, so the mapping layer had nothing to do.

interviewer_questions.question: "Why not JPA?"
interviewer_questions.answer: Every query here is a read-shaped derivation over two tables, not an object graph, and records already gave the mapping. It is also a divergence from the written decision, which I recorded on the decision rather than leaving the record wrong.

nodes.title: The runner is unsandboxed by design
nodes.statement: A local subprocess with a timeout (sweprep.grader.timeout, default PT10S) and a 1 MB captured-output cap. No container, no resource limits beyond that.
nodes.why_it_matters: This is sound because there is exactly one user running his own code, and the decision that makes it sound is written down along with what changes the moment the app is hosted. Runner being a small interface is the prepared answer to the follow-up.
nodes.how_to_say_it: It is not arbitrary code - it is one user running his own, locally. Safety today is a timeout and an output cap, the decision to skip a sandbox is recorded with what changes if it is ever hosted, and a container runner is a bean swap because Runner is an interface.

interviewer_questions.question: "You execute arbitrary code. How is that safe?"
interviewer_questions.answer: It is not arbitrary - one user, his own code, locally. Safety today is a timeout plus a 1 MB output cap; the decision to skip a sandbox is recorded with what changes if it is ever hosted, and a container runner is a bean swap.

evidence.note: MAX_CAPTURED_BYTES = 1 MB, shared by both local runners

nodes.title: Recompute-on-read everywhere
nodes.statement: Learned state, rep due dates, challenge priority, readiness and the streak (including its repair count) are all derived per request from attempt history rather than stored.
nodes.why_it_matters: Correct at this scale and it removes any possibility of drift between a cached summary and the history it summarises. It is a scaling question if the corpus ever gets large, and "there is exactly one user" is the honest reason it is fine today.
nodes.how_to_say_it: There is no spaced-repetition state to keep consistent, because there is no state - it is derived on read from the attempt history, so there is no second source of truth to drift.

interviewer_questions.question: "How do you keep the spaced-repetition state consistent?"
interviewer_questions.answer: There is no state to keep consistent. Learned state, due dates, priority and the streak are all derived on read from the attempt history, so there is no second source of truth to drift.

nodes.title: The real content is never verified in CI
nodes.statement: RealContentSmokeTest - the test that runs the answer-tell checker over the actual authored corpus - skips itself when no content clone is present, which is always the case in this repository's CI. The 5 skipped tests in the run above are exactly that.
nodes.why_it_matters: It is deliberate: an expected content failure must not wedge the engine's CI. It does mean the content-quality gates, which are the output of five separate tickets, run only where a clone exists.
nodes.how_to_say_it: A green suite is not evidence a named test ran. Those five skips are the content gates, and they are skipped by design - the argument for putting them in the content repo's own CI instead is the one I would make.

interviewer_questions.question: "How do you know your own content is any good?"
interviewer_questions.answer: By measuring exploit rates against a 25% baseline, finding a 41.2% one, fixing it in code and re-measuring. The honest caveat is that those gates skip in this repo's CI - a green suite is not evidence a named test ran.

nodes.title: The engine is built; the corpus it needs is not
nodes.statement: Issues #43 ("Author the AI/ML family, split by shelf life") and #44 ("Author the core and professional tranche, then the selected role families") are both open. The authoring tooling that derives warm-up reps from a reference solution landed at this SHA; the content it is meant to produce has not been authored.
nodes.why_it_matters: The planning map names content authoring as the most likely place this project stalls after the fun engineering is done, and the two open authoring tickets are that risk still standing. Naming your own project's biggest risk is a good answer, not a bad one.
nodes.how_to_say_it: The engine is ahead of the corpus. The tooling to derive reps mechanically is built precisely because authoring five items per problem by hand is the thing that would have killed this.

nodes.title: A machine-specific workaround is pinned in the build
nodes.statement: backend/pom.xml sets an api.version system property for Surefire because Testcontainers' Docker connectivity probe hardcodes an old API version that this dev machine's Docker Engine rejects outright. It is confirmed unnecessary on GitHub's hosted runners and kept anyway.
nodes.why_it_matters: It looks like stray config and is not. Knowing why a workaround exists before someone asks about it is the difference between a defensible build file and an unexplained one.
nodes.how_to_say_it: That property is a Testcontainers probe workaround for this box's Docker Engine, it is harmless where it is not needed, and it is documented in the project notes rather than left to be discovered.
